query.original_query: reasoning models reduce compute when tool or calculator available cognitive offloading test-time

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanistic interpretability of reasoning models using external tools or calculators to reduce test-time compute, cognitive offloading via tool use, circuit analysis of tool-augmented LLM reasoning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the mechanistic interpretability of tool-augmented language models, analyzing how internal circuits implement cognitive offloading during arithmetic reasoning. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize the model’s reliance on external calculators to specific attention heads and MLP layers within the residual stream. Our analysis reveals that when a tool is available, the model suppresses internal arithmetic computation in early layers, instead routing information through a distinct circuit that encodes the tool call and integrates the returned result. We find that this offloading behavior is mediated by a small set of attention heads that attend to the tool output token, effectively reducing the model’s reliance on its own parametric knowledge for factual recall. Further, we observe that the model’s internal representations of intermediate arithmetic steps become sparser and less polysemantic when the tool is used, consistent with a reduction in superposition. Results show that tool use does not merely add a post-hoc verification step but fundamentally alters the model’s internal reasoning trajectory, reducing test-time compute by shifting computation from the model’s weights to the external tool.

sub_queries.semantic_query: cognitive offloading using external tools and calculators to reduce mental computation demand, test-time resource allocation in human reasoning and problem-solving
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether individuals strategically offload cognitive demand onto external tools during arithmetic problem-solving, and whether this behavior reflects adaptive resource allocation under varying task constraints. Participants completed a series of multi-step calculation problems under high and low time pressure, with access to a physical calculator. We measured trial-by-trial calculator use, response time, and accuracy, and administered a self-report measure of perceived mental effort. Results indicate that calculator use increased significantly under high time pressure, particularly for problems with greater computational complexity. Accuracy was preserved when participants chose to offload, but response times were longer on offloaded trials, suggesting a speed-accuracy trade-off rather than pure efficiency gain. Findings support the hypothesis that cognitive offloading is a strategic, context-sensitive process governed by metacognitive evaluation of task demands and available cognitive resources. These results align with theories of distributed cognition and effort-based decision-making, and suggest that test-time resource allocation in human reasoning involves dynamic calibration between internal computation and external tool use.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Constructive Circuit Amplification: Improving Math Reasoning in LLMs via Targeted Sub-Network Updates
papers.research_question: How can we improve mathematical reasoning in LLMs by selectively updating the sparse subnetwork (circuit) responsible for correct reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constructive Circuit Amplification (CCA), a method that improves mathematical reasoning in LLMs by identifying and updating only the sparse subnetwork (circuit) responsible for correct reasoning, achieving significant accuracy gains with minimal impact on other abilities.
papers.conclusion: CCA substantially improves mathematical reasoning across multiple model families while modifying a small fraction of components, with minimal degradation on general-purpose benchmarks, demonstrating that model capabilities are often governed by sparse, localized subnetworks that can be selectively strengthened.
papers.key_findings:
CCA improves mathematical reasoning accuracy by up to +11.4% on GSM-Symbolic across multiple models.
CCA modifies as little as 1.59% of model components (attention heads and MLP neurons).
CCA preserves general abilities (MMLU, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA) with minimal degradation.
The Branching method for token localization consistently outperforms the Prefix method.
CCA outperforms LoRA fine-tuning in some models and is effective in data-constrained settings.
papers.limitation:
Focused on mathematical reasoning, leaving open whether similar gains can be achieved for other complex domains such as code generation or scientific problem solving.
Requires constructing error-localization datasets for token localization, which may be costly in settings without well-defined correctness signals.
Experiments considered only a single fine-tuning stage, whereas deployed models often undergo multiple rounds of fine-tuning.
future_direction: Extending CCA to other capabilities and domains, such as code generation, scientific reasoning, or multi-modal tasks.
Automating the error-localization process using frontier LLMs to reduce reliance on multiple generations and improve scalability.
Incorporating more sophisticated optimization techniques to refine model components more efficiently than naive gradient descent.
papers.abstract: Prior studies investigating the internal workings of LLMs have uncovered sparse subnetworks, often referred to as circuits, that are responsible for performing specific tasks. Additionally, it has been shown that model performance improvement through fine-tuning often results from the strengthening of existing circuits in the model. Taken together, these findings suggest the possibility of intervening directly on such circuits to make precise, task-targeted updates. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method called Constructive Circuit Amplification which identifies pivotal tokens from model reasoning traces as well as model components responsible for the desired task, and updates only those components. Applied to mathematical reasoning, it improves accuracy by up to +11.4% across multiple models while modifying as little as 1.59% of model components, with minimal impact on other abilities as measured by MMLU, TriviaQA, and TruthfulQA. These results demonstrate that targeted capabilities can be reliably enhanced by selectively updating a sparse set of model components.

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic reasoning tasks, and what circuits are responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers circuits in GPT-2 that explain its ability to perform syllogistic reasoning, including a novel negation mechanism for binary truth values.
papers.conclusion: The paper reverse-engineers GPT-2's handling of syllogistic reasoning, revealing circuits and negation mechanisms, and highlights the importance of interpretability for reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms that achieve high faithfulness to the full model.
Identified a negation mechanism where attention heads suppress truth logits and MLPs rescale to produce the opposite token.
Showed that components critical for one task have negative counterparts for opposite tasks, revealing how models handle binary pairs.
Found that the same heads can reverse their behavior between simple and opposite syllogism tasks.
Extended findings to larger models, showing variability in circuit behavior across scales.
papers.limitation: The understanding of model components' capabilities remains limited, indicating need for further research.
future_direction: Investigate how architectural scale affects circuit behavior.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous MI research has focused on linguistic tasks such as Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, e.g., "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is", which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that mechanistically explain GPT-2's logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token not present in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising five attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLPs in LMs. These insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and support future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Adaptive Tool Use in Large Language Models with Meta-Cognition Trigger
papers.research_question: How can large language models be guided to make adaptive decisions about when to use external tools, based on meta-cognitive self-assessment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MeCo, a fine-tuning-free adaptive tool-use strategy that uses meta-cognition probes to improve decision-making on when to invoke external tools, reducing latency and errors.
papers.conclusion: MeCo enhances decision accuracy for tool use and retrieval, demonstrating the utility of meta-cognition in LLM frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
MeCo reduces unnecessary tool invocations and latency compared to baselines.
It improves decision accuracy across multiple backbone models and benchmarks.
MeCo generalizes well to adaptive RAG scenarios.
The meta-cognition probe achieves high classification accuracy with minimal training data.
Fine-tuning and MeCo are orthogonal, with MeCo providing additional benefits to fine-tuned models.
papers.limitation: Evaluation focuses on decision-making rather than full end-to-end tool-use performance, including tool selection and parameter filling.
future_direction: Integrating MeCo into the full tool-use pipeline to handle downstream tasks like tool selection and parameter filling.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable emergent capabilities, transforming the execution of functional tasks by leveraging external tools for complex problems that require specialized processing or up-to-date data. While existing research expands LLMs access to diverse tools (e.g., program interpreters, search engines, calculators), the necessity of using these tools is often overlooked, leading to indiscriminate tool invocation. This naive approach raises two key issues: increased latency due to unnecessary tool calls, and potential errors resulting from faulty interactions with external tools. In this paper, we introduce meta-cognition as a proxy for LLMs self-assessment of their capabilities, reflecting the model's awareness of its own limitations. Based on this, we propose MeCo, an adaptive decision-making strategy for external tool use. MeCo quantifies metacognitive scores by capturing high-level cognitive signals in the representation space, guiding when to invoke tools. Notably, MeCo is fine-tuning-free and incurs minimal cost. Experiments across multiple backbone models and benchmarks show that MeCo reliably detects LLMs' internal cognitive signals and significantly improves tool-use decision-making.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs struggle to detect arithmetic errors in their own outputs, and what internal mechanisms are responsible for error detection?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have a structural dissociation between arithmetic computation (in higher layers) and validation (in middle layers), relying on consistency heads for surface-level alignment checks, which explains their difficulty in error detection.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability provides valuable insights into how LLMs detect or fail to detect arithmetic errors, and the validation gap arises from structural dissociation between computation and validation.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for arithmetic error detection are structurally similar across different models.
Error detection is governed by consistency heads—attention heads in lower to middle layers that check surface-level alignment of numerical values.
Arithmetic computation occurs in higher layers, while validation takes place in middle layers, leading to a structural dissociation.
Patching a small subset of consistency heads can control the model's error detection behavior.
Adding latent activations from higher layers to the residual stream in lower layers significantly enhances error detection, closing the validation gap.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to smaller LLMs and basic math word problems.
Circuit discovery may not be complete, i.e., identified circuits might not include all components involved in the task behavior.
future_direction: Study error detection in larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to validate their output and identify potential errors is crucial for ensuring robustness and reliability. However, current research indicates that LLMs struggle with self-correction, encountering significant challenges in detecting errors. While studies have explored methods to enhance self-correction in LLMs, relatively little attention has been given to understanding the models' internal mechanisms underlying error detection. In this paper, we present a mechanistic analysis of error detection in LLMs, focusing on simple arithmetic problems. Through circuit analysis, we identify the computational subgraphs responsible for detecting arithmetic errors across four smaller-sized LLMs. Our findings reveal that all models heavily rely on $\textit{consistency heads}$--attention heads that assess surface-level alignment of numerical values in arithmetic solutions. Moreover, we observe that the models' internal arithmetic computation primarily occurs in higher layers, whereas validation takes place in middle layers, before the final arithmetic results are fully encoded. This structural dissociation between arithmetic computation and validation seems to explain why smaller-sized LLMs struggle to detect even simple arithmetic errors.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Understanding Addition and Subtraction in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn exact arithmetic algorithms for addition and subtraction, and how do they implement these algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformers can learn exact addition and subtraction algorithms with near-perfect accuracy, and these algorithms are implemented via interpretable circuits in attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement exact n-digit addition and subtraction through interpretable circuits, and with appropriate training, larger LLMs could in principle adopt the same mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Small transformers (2-3 layers, 3-4 heads) achieve >99.999% accuracy on n-digit addition and subtraction.
The models implement specific algorithms for addition and subtraction based on cascading carry and borrow circuits.
Mixed models initialized with addition weights can reuse circuits for subtraction, with many nodes becoming polysemantic.
Only 7% of 180 surveyed public LLMs can reliably perform addition without external tools.
The algorithmic implementation is consistent across seeds and model sizes, with attention heads and MLPs satisfying strict constraints.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not examine the specific data representations and transformations used by polysemantic nodes, SGN nodes, and OPR nodes in the residual stream, nor the detailed mechanisms of MLP layers.
The automated framework for discovering algorithm subtasks has limitations and some aspects are specific to the math models studied.
Fully reverse engineering neural networks is challenging due to distributed parallel computations difficult to trace to specific components.
future_direction: Refine the declarative language for describing algorithms and the framework for testing these descriptions against models.
Further work to understand how identified components actually encode and manipulate information.
Investigate the universality of representations and circuits across models using the provided models.
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely deployed in large language models (LLMs), yet most models still fail on basic arithmetic tasks such as multidigit addition. In contrast, we show that small transformers trained from scratch can solve n-digit addition and subtraction with 99.999% accuracy. Building directly on prior work that uncovered addition circuits, we extend the analysis to subtraction and present a unified mechanistic account based on cascading carry and borrow circuits. Using a suite of 49 trained models, we apply systematic ablations and node-level constraints to validate the learned mechanisms and release a reproducible interpretability toolkit for studying arithmetic circuits. Finally, surveying 180 publicly available LLMs, we find that only 7% can reliably perform addition, underscoring the gap between specialized small models and general-purpose LLMs. Our results show that arithmetic can be implemented exactly by tiny transformers, offering a tractable case study for mechanistic interpretability and a cautionary contrast with the persistent arithmetic failures of much larger models.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model perform multi-step reasoning by recalling memorized information or by following a step-by-step reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that language models perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning tree information can often be detected from attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that encode reasoning information degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with better accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The work considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
Analysis of multi-head attention is limited; shallow models with many heads might have different head functions.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models (LMs) have strong multi-step (i.e., procedural) reasoning capabilities. However, it is unclear whether LMs perform these tasks by cheating with answers memorized from pretraining corpus, or, via a multi-step reasoning mechanism. In this paper, we try to answer this question by exploring a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks. Concretely, we hypothesize that the LM implicitly embeds a reasoning tree resembling the correct reasoning process within it. We test this hypothesis by introducing a new probing approach (called MechanisticProbe) that recovers the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns. We use our probe to analyze two LMs: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter & AI2 Reasoning Challenge). We show that MechanisticProbe is able to detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for most examples, suggesting that the LM indeed is going through a process of multi-step reasoning within its architecture in many cases.

papers.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does modular training (BIMT) affect the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery? How does modularity impact computational efficiency (training memory, time, inference)?
papers.core_contribution: Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) significantly improves the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery, producing sparser circuits with lower logit differences and faster discovery times, though with increased training memory and time.
papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed. This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: Can LLMs Reason Abstractly Over Math Word Problems Without CoT? Disentangling Abstract Formulation From Arithmetic Computation
papers.research_question: Does final-answer accuracy in math word problems conflate abstract formulation and arithmetic computation? What is the internal mechanism of LLMs when solving such problems without chain-of-thought?
papers.core_contribution: Disentangled evaluation shows that without CoT, models' final-answer accuracy is bottlenecked by arithmetic computation, not abstract formulation, and mechanistic analysis reveals an abstract-then-compute mechanism in a single forward pass.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled evaluation reveals that without CoT, models perform better at abstraction than computation, challenging the view that poor performance always implies reasoning failure. Mechanistic interpretability uncovers an abstract-then-compute mechanism with transferable abstractions, arguing for disentangled evaluation to assess model abilities more precisely.
papers.key_findings:
Without CoT, models perform better at abstract formulation than arithmetic computation, with computation being the main bottleneck for final-answer accuracy.
CoT primarily improves computation, with limited gains in abstract formulation.
Models use an abstract-then-compute mechanism in a single forward pass, where abstractions are formed first and then used for computation.
Abstractions are transferable across problem variants and can be composed with subsequent computation.
The abstract-then-compute mechanism is consistent across different models and problem types.
papers.limitation:
Focus solely on English-language datasets.
Evaluation decomposes mathematical problem-solving into only two stages: abstract formulation and arithmetic computation.
Interpretability analysis is limited to single-step generation.
Detailed analysis of components (e.g., attention heads, MLP neurons) is left for future work.
Analysis is limited to models up to 12B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending interpretability techniques to multi-step reasoning.
Extending analysis to larger models.
Investigating finer-grained breakdowns of mathematical problem-solving.
papers.abstract: Final-answer-based metrics are commonly used for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on math word problems, often taken as proxies for reasoning ability. However, such metrics conflate two distinct sub-skills: abstract formulation (capturing mathematical relationships using expressions) and arithmetic computation (executing the calculations). Through a disentangled evaluation on GSM8K and SVAMP, we find that the final-answer accuracy of Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 (1B-32B) without CoT is overwhelmingly bottlenecked by the arithmetic computation step and not by the abstract formulation step. Contrary to the common belief, we show that CoT primarily aids in computation, with limited impact on abstract formulation. Mechanistically, we show that these two skills are composed conjunctively even in a single forward pass without any reasoning steps via an abstract-then-compute mechanism: models first capture problem abstractions, then handle computation. Causal patching confirms these abstractions are present, transferable, composable, and precede computation. These behavioural and mechanistic findings highlight the need for disentangled evaluation to accurately assess LLM reasoning and to guide future improvements.

papers.title: Extracting Interpretable Task-Specific Circuits from Large Language Models for Faster Inference
papers.research_question: Is it possible to extract the minimal subset from an LLM that is able to perform a specific task in a faster, standalone manner?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel method to automatically extract task-specific circuits from large language models without additional training, resulting in smaller, faster, and more interpretable submodels.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully extracts task-specific circuits from LLMs, enabling standalone usage with reduced size and inference time, and aligns with prior circuit identification results.
papers.key_findings:
The pruned models achieve up to 82.77% reduction in parameters while maintaining or improving task accuracy.
Mean ablation yields smaller models than zero ablation with better performance consistency.
The extracted circuits include most important components identified in previous manual circuit analyses.
Pruning irrelevant attention heads is prioritized over MLPs in the extraction process.
The method outperforms knowledge distillation with small data samples.
future_direction: Metric selection for different tasks
Study of phenomena like accuracy-KL divergence correlation in greater-than task
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks. However, the size of LLMs is steadily increasing, hindering their application on computationally constrained environments. On the other hand, despite their general capabilities, there are many situations where only one specific task is performed, rendering all other capabilities unnecessary and wasteful. This leads us to the following question: Is it possible to extract the minimal subset from an LLM that is able to perform a specific task in a faster, standalone manner? Recent works on Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) have shown that specific tasks are performed by a localized subset of components, or circuit. However, current techniques used to identify the circuit cannot be used to extract it for its standalone usage. In this work, we propose a novel approach to automatically extract the subset of the LLM that properly performs a targeted task requiring no additional training and a small amount of data samples. We evaluate our approach on different tasks and show that the resulting models are (i) considerably smaller, reducing the number of parameters up to 82.77% and (ii) more interpretable, as they focus on the circuit that is used to carry out the specific task, and can therefore be understood using MI techniques.

papers.title: Modular Arithmetic: Language Models Solve Math Digit by Digit
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms do LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, specifically focusing on whether they employ digit-position-specific circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates digit-position-specific arithmetic circuits in LLMs, showing that LLMs solve arithmetic tasks digit by digit using modular circuits that causally control individual output digits.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform simple arithmetic using modular, digit-position-specific circuits that operate independently, indicating a structured and compositional approach to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs use distinct, digit-position-specific circuits for units, tens, and hundreds digits in addition and subtraction.
These circuits are causally involved, as targeted interventions selectively alter only the corresponding digit in the output.
The circuits exist across various model sizes and tokenization strategies, including both multi-digit and single-digit tokenization.
Addition and subtraction circuits rely on largely distinct sets of neurons.
Carry operations are handled separately from the digit-position circuits, suggesting additional mechanisms for carry propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to addition and subtraction, not addressing more complex operations like multiplication or division.
Focuses on MLP layers and does not account for the role of attention heads or other residual stream components.
Uses Fisher Score for neuron identification, which may not be the most precise method compared to gradient-based attribution.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Analyzing circuits responsible for composing digit-level results into final outputs.
Using more precise methods like gradient-based attribution for circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: While recent work has begun to uncover the internal strategies that Large Language Models (LLMs) employ for simple arithmetic tasks, a unified understanding of their underlying mechanisms is still lacking. We extend recent findings showing that LLMs represent numbers in a digit-wise manner and present evidence for the existence of digit-position-specific circuits that LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, i.e. modular subgroups of MLP neurons that operate independently on different digit positions (units, tens, hundreds). Notably, such circuits exist independently of model size and of tokenization strategy, i.e. both for models that encode longer numbers digit-by-digit and as one token. Using Feature Importance and Causal Interventions, we identify and validate the digit-position-specific circuits, revealing a compositional and interpretable structure underlying the solving of arithmetic problems in LLMs. Our interventions selectively alter the model's prediction at targeted digit positions, demonstrating the causal role of digit-position circuits in solving arithmetic tasks.

papers.title: CircuitSeer: Mining High-Quality Data by Probing Mathematical Reasoning Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we select high-quality reasoning data for fine-tuning LLMs by leveraging the model's internal mechanisms, specifically sparse, specialized attention circuits, instead of relying on external heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CircuitSeer, a data selection method that quantifies reasoning complexity by measuring the influence of training samples on sparse, specialized attention head circuits identified within a reference LLM, enabling efficient fine-tuning with small, high-quality subsets.
papers.conclusion: CircuitSeer provides an interpretable, model-internal signal for reasoning data quality, enabling efficient and effective data selection for fine-tuning LLMs, and demonstrates that internal reasoning circuits encode measurable structures of problem difficulty.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse, specialized subset of attention heads forms core reasoning circuits that are consistently activated during complex mathematical reasoning tasks.
Fine-tuning on just 10% of data selected by CircuitSeer can outperform training on the full dataset, achieving a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
Scoring based on input problem statements (rather than output reasoning traces) more effectively captures reasoning complexity.
Soft sampling based on CircuitSeer scores yields better performance and diversity than deterministic top-k selection.
The identified reasoning heads provide a clearer signal for data selection than using all heads or a random subset.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, but scaling their performance often relies on massive reasoning datasets that are computationally expensive to train on. Existing data selection methods aim to curate smaller, high-quality subsets but often rely on costly external models or opaque heuristics. In this work, we shift the focus from external heuristics to the model's internal mechanisms. We find that complex reasoning tasks consistently activate a sparse, specialized subset of attention heads, forming core reasoning circuits. Building on this insight, we propose CircuitSeer, a novel data selection method that quantifies the reasoning complexity of data by measuring its influence on these crucial circuits. Extensive experiments on 4 models and 9 datasets demonstrate CircuitSeer's superiority. Notably, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B on just 10% of data selected by our method achieves a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 over training on the full dataset, highlighting its efficiency and effectiveness.

papers.title: Free(): Learning to Forget in Malloc-Only Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How can we address the performance degradation in reasoning models caused by excessive accumulation of thinking tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Free()LM, a method that adds a self-forgetting capability to LLMs via a plug-and-play LoRA adapter (Free-Module) to dynamically prune redundant context during reasoning, improving performance and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Sustainable long-horizon intelligence requires models to actively forget redundant information, not just accumulate it; Free()LM provides a practical method to achieve this.
papers.key_findings:
Free()LM consistently improves reasoning accuracy across model scales (8B to 685B) while reducing context length.
Free()LM recovers performance on long-horizon tasks where standard models suffer catastrophic degradation (e.g., from 0% to ~50% accuracy).
The trained Free-Module generalizes across different model architectures (e.g., from Qwen to DeepSeek).
Heuristic compression methods (H2O, ThinkCleary) fail to improve accuracy and can cause catastrophic degeneration.
Free()LM maintains performance on short-reasoning tasks, showing no degradation in general capabilities.
papers.limitation:
Free()LM incurs a 56% latency overhead per sample due to decoding free() commands and re-prefilling after deletion.
There is a risk of over-pruning, which can force the model to regenerate previously deleted content.
future_direction: Implementing KV Cache Pruning (Strategy 2) to reduce latency overhead.
Deploying the Free-Module as a 'Universal Context Pruning Service' for any backbone model.
papers.abstract: Reasoning models enhance problem-solving by scaling test-time compute, yet they face a critical paradox: excessive thinking tokens often degrade performance rather than improve it. We attribute this to a fundamental architectural flaw: standard LLMs operate as "malloc-only" engines, continuously accumulating valid and redundant steps alike without a mechanism to prune obsolete information. To break this cycle, we propose Free()LM, a model that introduces an intrinsic self-forgetting capability via the Free-Module, a plug-and-play LoRA adapter. By iteratively switching between reasoning and cleaning modes, Free()LM dynamically identifies and prunes useless context chunks, maintaining a compact and noise-free state. Extensive experiments show that Free()LM provides consistent improvements across all model scales (8B to 685B). It achieves a 3.3% average improvement over top-tier reasoning baselines, even establishing a new SOTA on IMOanswerBench using DeepSeek V3.2-Speciale. Most notably, in long-horizon tasks where the standard Qwen3-235B-A22B model suffers a total collapse (0% accuracy), Free()LM restores performance to 50%. Our findings suggest that sustainable intelligence requires the freedom to forget as much as the power to think.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering the Cognitive Behaviors of Reasoning Models at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks. While effective, these trajectories are frequently inefficient, leading to high latency from excessive token generation, or unstable reasoning that alternates between underthinking (shallow, inconsistent steps) and overthinking (repetitive, verbose reasoning). In this work, we study the structure of reasoning trajectories and uncover specialized attention heads that correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. By lightly intervening on these heads at inference time, we can steer the model away from inefficient modes. Building on this insight, we propose CREST, a training-free method for Cognitive REasoning Steering at Test-time. CREST has two components: (1) an offline calibration step that identifies cognitive heads and derives head-specific steering vectors, and (2) an inference-time procedure that rotates hidden representations to suppress components along those vectors. CREST adaptively suppresses unproductive reasoning behaviors, yielding both higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and models, CREST improves accuracy by up to 17.5% while reducing token usage by 37.6%, offering a simple and effective pathway to faster, more reliable LLM reasoning.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
