The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Mitigating Cognitive Inertia in Large Reasoning Models via Latent Spike Steering
papers.research_question: How can cognitive inertia (overthinking and reasoning rigidity) in Large Reasoning Models be mitigated by monitoring and steering latent dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STARS, a training-free framework that detects Cognitive Pivots via L2 distance spikes in hidden states and uses geometric trajectory analysis to diagnose and steer reasoning in real-time, mitigating cognitive inertia.
papers.conclusion: STARS effectively mitigates cognitive inertia in LRMs by detecting latent spikes and steering reasoning trajectories, offering a robust, unsupervised mechanism to optimize the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
STARS improves accuracy while reducing unnecessary token usage across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
STARS mitigates both overthinking (inertia of motion) and reasoning rigidity (inertia of direction).
STARS generalizes to non-mathematical domains such as logical puzzles and scientific reasoning.
STARS achieves lower tail latency and higher decoding throughput compared to token-level baselines like DEER and ConCISE.
The framework is training-free and does not require fine-tuning, operating solely at inference time.
papers.limitation:
When the model terminates reasoning before any salient latent spike occurs, no intervention can be triggered.
A detected spike may occasionally redirect the model toward an incorrect alternative trajectory, reinforcing rather than rectifying the error.
Spike-based signals may be less pronounced or harder to exploit in models with compressed representations, limited capacity, or training objectives that encourage smoother internal dynamics.
papers.abstract: While Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable performance by scaling test-time compute, they frequently suffer from Cognitive Inertia, a failure pattern manifesting as either overthinking (inertia of motion) or reasoning rigidity (inertia of direction). Existing detection methods, typically relying on superficial textual heuristics like self-correction tokens, often fail to capture the model's unvoiced internal conflicts. To address this, we propose STARS (Spike-Triggered Adaptive Reasoning Steering), a training-free framework designed to rectify cognitive inertia by monitoring latent dynamics. STARS identifies Cognitive Pivots-critical moments of reasoning transition-by detecting distinct L2 distance spikes in the hidden states. Upon detection, the framework employs geometric trajectory analysis to diagnose the structural nature of the transition and injects state-aware language cues to steer the model in real-time. Our experiments across diverse benchmarks confirm that STARS efficiently curtails redundant loops while improving accuracy through the adaptive correction of erroneous trajectories. STARS offers a robust, unsupervised mechanism to optimize the reasoning process of LRMs without requiring additional fine-tuning.

papers.title: RADAR: Mechanistic Pathways for Detecting Data Contamination in LLM Evaluation
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to detect data contamination in LLM evaluation by distinguishing recall-based from reasoning-based model responses?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RADAR, a framework that uses mechanistic interpretability to detect data contamination in LLMs by analyzing internal activation patterns to distinguish recall-based from reasoning-based responses, achieving 93% accuracy.
papers.conclusion: RADAR demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can effectively detect data contamination by analyzing internal LLM processing signatures, achieving high accuracy and providing interpretable insights, opening new directions for LLM evaluation beyond surface-level metrics.
papers.key_findings:
RADAR achieves 93% overall accuracy in distinguishing recall from reasoning, with 100% accuracy on clear cases and 76.7% on challenging ambiguous examples.
Recall tasks exhibit focused attention patterns, rapid confidence convergence, and higher specialized head counts.
Reasoning tasks show distributed attention, gradual confidence build-up, and higher circuit complexity.
Key discriminative features include specialized attention heads, circuit complexity, and hidden state variance.
The method works without access to training data and provides interpretable insights into model internal processes.
papers.limitation:
Several features rely on proxy measures rather than direct computation, such as causal effects derived from attention entropy instead of actual interventions.
Activation patching is approximated via attention entropy proxy, not true patching experiments.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models.
Developing unsupervised detection methods.
Extending to other contamination types.
papers.abstract: Data contamination poses a significant challenge to reliable LLM evaluation, where models may achieve high performance by memorizing training data rather than demonstrating genuine reasoning capabilities. We introduce RADAR (Recall vs. Reasoning Detection through Activation Representation), a novel framework that leverages mechanistic interpretability to detect contamination by distinguishing recall-based from reasoning-based model responses. RADAR extracts 37 features spanning surface-level confidence trajectories and deep mechanistic properties including attention specialization, circuit dynamics, and activation flow patterns. Using an ensemble of classifiers trained on these features, RADAR achieves 93\% accuracy on a diverse evaluation set, with perfect performance on clear cases and 76.7\% accuracy on challenging ambiguous examples. This work demonstrates the potential of mechanistic interpretability for advancing LLM evaluation beyond traditional surface-level metrics.

papers.title: I Have Covered All the Bases Here: Interpreting Reasoning Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities internally encoded within large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ReasonScore, an automatic metric to identify reasoning features in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, and provides causal evidence that amplifying these features improves reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a first step towards a mechanistic understanding of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ReasonScore identifies SAE features corresponding to uncertainty, exploration, and reflection.
Steering these features improves performance on reasoning benchmarks and leads to longer reasoning traces.
These reasoning features are present only in models with reasoning capabilities, as shown by model diffing.
papers.abstract: Recent LLMs like DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance by integrating deep thinking and complex reasoning during generation. However, the internal mechanisms behind these reasoning processes remain unexplored. We observe reasoning LLMs consistently use vocabulary associated with human reasoning processes. We hypothesize these words correspond to specific reasoning moments within the models' internal mechanisms. To test this hypothesis, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), a technique for sparse decomposition of neural network activations into human-interpretable features. We introduce ReasonScore, an automatic metric to identify active SAE features during these reasoning moments. We perform manual and automatic interpretation of the features detected by our metric, and find those with activation patterns matching uncertainty, exploratory thinking, and reflection. Through steering experiments, we demonstrate that amplifying these features increases performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks (+2.2%) while producing longer reasoning traces (+20.5%). Using the model diffing technique, we provide evidence that these features are present only in models with reasoning capabilities. Our work provides the first step towards a mechanistic understanding of reasoning in LLMs. Code available at https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/SAE-Reasoning

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Improving Chain-of-Thought for Logical Reasoning via Attention-Aware Intervention
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode and utilize structural information in their latent representations for logical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), a non-interactive, end-to-end framework that reweights attention scores to steer LLMs' reasoning for improved logical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: AAI effectively improves logical reasoning in LLMs by reweighting attention scores based on identified patterns, achieving competitive performance with low overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in LLMs exhibit structured activation patterns (anchor, aggregation, copy heads) when symbolic structures are injected into prompts.
Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI) reweights attention scores to reinforce linkages between rule identifiers and their content, improving reasoning.
AAI improves accuracy on logical reasoning benchmarks like ProofWriter, ProntoQA, Logical Deduction, and FOLIO across various LLMs.
The method scales well with model size and generalizes to mathematical reasoning tasks like GSM8k.
AAI incurs negligible additional computational overhead during inference.
papers.abstract: Modern logical reasoning with LLMs primarily relies on employing complex interactive frameworks that decompose the reasoning process into subtasks solved through carefully designed prompts or requiring external resources (e.g., symbolic solvers) to exploit their strong logical structures. While interactive approaches introduce additional overhead or depend on external components, which limit their scalability. In this work, we introduce a non-interactive, end-to-end framework for reasoning tasks, enabling reasoning to emerge within the model itself-improving generalization while preserving analyzability without any external resources. We show that introducing structural information into the few-shot prompt activates a subset of attention heads that patterns aligned with logical reasoning operators. Building on this insight, we propose Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), an inference-time intervention method that reweights attention scores across selected heads identified by their logical patterns. AAI offers an efficient way to steer the model's reasoning toward leveraging prior knowledge through attention modulation. Extensive experiments show that AAI enhances logical reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks, and model architectures, while incurring negligible additional computational overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/phuongnm94/aai_for_logical_reasoning.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
papers.conclusion: PAHQ provides an efficient acceleration approach for mechanistic interpretability research without sacrificing analytical quality, making circuit discovery more computationally feasible.
papers.key_findings:
PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80% and memory consumption by up to 30% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness.
PAHQ outperforms RTN quantization and Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) in terms of AUC-ROC on circuit discovery tasks like IOI, Docstring, and Greater Than.
The method is training-free and readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism.
PAHQ's selective precision allocation and three-stream parallel scheduler effectively mask data transfer latency, enabling near-optimal throughput.
The method scales effectively to larger transformer models (GPT-2-medium, large, XL) while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
PAHQ is designed for algorithms that evaluate edges sequentially (like ACDC) and may not be as effective for methods that evaluate multiple edges simultaneously (like EAP).
PAHQ makes circuit discovery more feasible for moderately larger models but does not solve the scalability challenge for foundation models with hundreds of billions of parameters.
The method is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis on how high-precision signals propagate through lower-precision layers.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery, which involves identifying sparse and task-relevant subnetworks in pre-trained language models, is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in circuit discovery, but its application to large language models is severely limited by computational inefficiency and prohibitively high memory requirements. Although several accelerated approaches have been proposed, they primarily rely on linear approximations to ACDC, which significantly compromises analytical faithfulness. Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form during a training phase change that coincides with a dramatic improvement in in-context learning.
Architectural perturbations that shift induction head formation also shift in-context learning improvements accordingly.
Ablating induction heads in small models significantly reduces in-context learning ability.
Induction heads can implement abstract behaviors like translation and pattern matching, suggesting generality beyond literal copying.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models is plausible for general in-context learning, and behaviors are continuous from small to large models.
papers.limitation: Evidence is preliminary and indirect, especially for large models, with potential confounds or alternative hypotheses.
future_direction: Future work could build on these results to establish the claim more firmly.
Studying phase changes up close may offer generalizable lessons for safety in machine learning systems.
papers.abstract: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models? This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models. The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.

papers.title: KV Cache Steering for Controlling Frozen LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we develop lightweight, post-training interventions to unlock and steer inherent reasoning processes in language models, specifically via a one-shot modification of the key-value cache?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cache steering, a one-shot method for steering language model behavior by modifying the key-value cache, which is more efficient and stable than continuous activation steering and does not require fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Cache steering provides a lightweight, practical mechanism for behavior-level guidance of language models, offering a stable and efficient alternative to activation steering and fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Cache steering induces chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models without fine-tuning or prompt modifications.
The method improves reasoning structure and task performance on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC-c, CSQA, PIQA).
Cache steering is more computationally efficient and stable to hyperparameters than activation steering.
The technique enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical) from teacher models.
The method scales to larger models and yields gains on challenging datasets like GPQA and MATH.
papers.limitation:
Further study is needed to assess how well cache steering generalizes across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
Potential misuse, such as steering toward deceptive, harmful, or biased outputs, remains a concern.
future_direction: Further study to assess generalization across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
papers.abstract: We propose cache steering, a lightweight method for implicit steering of language models via a one-shot intervention applied directly to the key-value cache. To validate its effectiveness, we apply cache steering to induce chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models. Our approach constructs steering vectors from reasoning traces, obtained either from teacher models (e.g., GPT-4o) or existing human annotations, that shift model behavior toward more explicit, multi-step reasoning without fine-tuning or prompt modifications. Experimental evaluations on diverse reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that cache steering improves both the qualitative structure of model reasoning and quantitative task performance. Additional experiments show that the method also scales to larger models and yields further gains on challenging datasets such as GPQA and MATH. Compared to prior activation steering techniques that require continuous interventions, our one-shot cache steering offers substantial advantages in terms of inference latency, hyperparameter stability, and ease of integration with existing inference APIs. Beyond mere reasoning induction, we show that cache steering enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical), making it a practical tool for behavior-level guidance of language models.

papers.title: CircuChain: Disentangling Competence and Compliance in LLM Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can adhere to user-specified conventions in circuit analysis or if they default to learned priors, disentangling physical reasoning competence from instruction compliance.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CircuChain, a benchmark to disentangle instruction compliance from physical reasoning competence in LLMs for circuit analysis, and reveals that stronger models exhibit higher physical reasoning but lower compliance with user-defined conventions.
papers.conclusion: CircuChain reveals a reliability gap where numerical correctness is insufficient without adherence to user-declared conventions, highlighting the need for compliance-aware evaluation and training in safety-critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.5 achieve comparable overall accuracy but differ in error types, with GPT-5 having high compliance errors and no competence errors, while Claude Opus 4.5 has lower compliance errors but higher competence errors.
There is a compliance-competence trade-off: increased model capability does not guarantee improved adherence to user-defined conventions.
Performance varies by circuit topology, with ladder circuits being solved most accurately and T-networks being most challenging.
Models show robustness differences under Trap regimes, with Claude Opus 4.5 performing better on Traps than Controls, while others degrade.
The benchmark reveals that numerical correctness is insufficient without procedural fidelity to conventions.
papers.limitation:
CircuChain currently covers only five linear circuit topologies and evaluates text-only reasoning under a fixed convention contract.
Failure attribution uses an LLM-based judge, which, while audited, may have limitations in error classification.
future_direction: Expanding to richer topologies, such as op-amp circuits, AC/phasor analysis, and diagram-grounded inputs.
Incorporating additional auditors and rule-based checks for error attribution to improve reliability.
Extending CircuChain to compare performance under different convention contracts.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward expert-level performance in engineering domains, reliable reasoning under user-specified constraints becomes critical. In circuit analysis, for example, a numerically correct solution is insufficient if it violates established methodological conventions such as mesh directionality or polarity assignments, errors that can propagate in safety-critical systems. Yet it remains unclear whether frontier models truly apply first-principles reasoning or rely on entrenched training priors that conflict with explicit instructions. We introduce CircuChain, a diagnostic benchmark designed to disentangle instruction compliance from physical reasoning competence in electrical circuit analysis. CircuChain consists of counterbalanced Control/Trap problem pairs across five canonical circuit topologies, augmented with systematic variations in sign conventions, current orientations, and polarity definitions. A multi-stage verification pipeline, combining symbolic solvers, SPICE simulation, and an LLM-based error taxonomy, enables fine-grained attribution of failures to convention errors, physics errors, arithmetic mistakes, or hallucinations. Across 100 tasks per model, we observe a consistent Compliance-Competence Divergence. The strongest model evaluated exhibits near-perfect physical reasoning but a high rate of convention violations when Trap conditions deliberately invert natural sign patterns. Conversely, weaker models display lower physical fidelity yet superior adherence to explicit instructions. These results suggest that increased model capability does not guarantee improved constraint alignment and highlight the need for new evaluation frameworks that stress instruction-following under mathematically rigid domains. CircuChain provides one such framework and offers actionable insights for both engineering education and AI alignment research.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Arithmetic Word Problems
papers.research_question: How do chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts improve LLMs' accuracy on arithmetic word problems, and do LLMs actually use their CoTs to reason to their final answers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that CoT-prompted LLMs use their generated chain-of-thought tokens to reason to final answers in arithmetic word problems, as shown through causal abstraction analysis.
papers.conclusion: LLMs achieve higher accuracy with CoT prompting, correct answers correlate with correct CoTs, and LLMs partially realize the causal models from their CoTs, suggesting they use CoTs to reason, though for some LLMs other processes may also play a role.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting significantly improves LLM accuracy on the GSM8K test set compared to non-CoT prompting.
Correct final answers are highly correlated with correctly formulated and executed CoTs.
LLMs realize the causal models suggested by their CoTs to a fairly large extent, indicating causal impact of CoT tokens on final answers.
For Cohere Command and PaLM Bison, higher degrees of realization are associated with better overall accuracy.
For OpenAI GPT-3.5, other internal processes may be involved, as shown by intervention-ignoring and self-correcting behavior.
papers.limitation:
Only examines a few LLMs' behavior for a small subset of examples from a single dataset.
Limited to one type of reasoning task (multi-step arithmetic) and may not generalize to other tasks.
Experiments conducted in a controlled setting with temperature 0, so findings may not extend to settings with randomness.
Only found evidence of partial realizations, and the theoretical interpretation of such partial realizations is unclear.
future_direction: Scale up to more examples with more robust human evaluation methods.
Explore cases where LLMs produce incorrect CoTs to examine if they still realize the causal models.
Replicate experiments with LLMs whose internal representations are accessible.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) achieve higher accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks when prompted to generate intermediate reasoning steps, or a chain of thought (CoT), before their final answer. However, it is unclear how exactly CoTs improve LLMs’ accuracy, and in particular, if LLMs use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. This paper tries to answer this question with respect to arithmetic word problems, by (i) evaluating the correctness of LLMs’ CoTs, and (ii) using causal abstraction to assess if the intermediate tokens produced as part of a CoT causally impact LLMs’ final answers, in line with the reasoning described by the CoT. We find that for CoT-prompted LLMs, correct answers to arithmetic problems are highly correlated with correct CoTs, and that when LLMs produce correct CoTs, they realize to a fairly large extent the causal models suggested by their CoTs. Higher degrees of realization also seem associated with better overall accuracy on the arithmetic problems. These findings suggest that some CoT-prompted LLMs may do better on multi-step arithmetic reasoning at least partly because they use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. However, for some LLMs, other internal processes may also be involved.

papers.title: A Causal Framework to Quantify the Robustness of Mathematical Reasoning with Language Models
papers.research_question: How robust is the mathematical reasoning of language models on math word problems, and what are the causal effects of input factors (e.g., surface form, operands, operators) on the model's solution?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal framework to quantify the robustness and sensitivity of language models on math word problems, finding that GPT-3 Davinci models show dramatic improvement in both aspects compared to other GPT variants.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a causal framework for behavioral analysis of language models on math word problems, revealing that robustness does not continuously improve with size, but GPT-3 Davinci models show significant improvement, though performance degrades on more complex problems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger non-instruction-tuned models tend to be more sensitive to changes in the ground-truth result, but not necessarily more robust.
GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.
Instruction tuning (as in GPT-3 Davinci) improves robustness and sensitivity, but the type of instruction tuning matters.
For three-operand problems, even the best models (GPT-3 Davinci) show a significant degradation in robustness.
The causal framework allows disentangling the direct and total causal effects of operands (N) and textual surface form (S) on model predictions.
papers.limitation:
The numerical space for operands is limited to integers up to 300 to ensure numbers are represented as single tokens.
For GPT-3, the API only returns top-k logits, so causal effect metrics (δrcc) are approximated.
The LLaMA tokenizer treats each digit as a separate token, making probability comparison for multi-digit numbers problematic.
future_direction: Examine different types of instruction tuning (e.g., focused on reasoning procedures or reinforcement learning from human feedback).
Extend the framework to more complex problems (e.g., with more operands or different types of math problems).
papers.abstract: We have recently witnessed a number of impressive results on hard mathematical reasoning problems with language models. At the same time, the robustness of these models has also been called into question; recent works have shown that models can rely on shallow patterns in the problem description when generating a solution. Building on the idea of behavioral testing, we propose a novel framework, which pins down the causal effect of various factors in the input, e.g., the surface form of the problem text, the operands, and math operators on the output solution. By grounding the behavioral analysis in a causal graph describing an intuitive reasoning process, we study the behavior of language models in terms of robustness and sensitivity to direct interventions in the input space. We apply our framework on a test bed of math word problems. Our analysis shows that robustness does not appear to continuously improve as a function of size, but the GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection for Efficient Reasoning in Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel at solving complex problems by explicitly generating a reasoning trace before deriving the final answer. However, these extended generations incur substantial memory footprint and computational overhead, bottlenecking LRMs' efficiency. This work uses attention maps to analyze the influence of reasoning traces and uncover an interesting phenomenon: only some decision-critical tokens in a reasoning trace steer the model toward the final answer, while the remaining tokens contribute negligibly. Building on this observation, we propose Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection (DynTS). This method identifies decision-critical tokens and retains only their associated Key-Value (KV) cache states during inference, evicting the remaining redundant entries to optimize efficiency.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Open-sourcing circuit-tracing tools
papers.core_contribution: This blog post announces the open-source release of circuit-tracing tools that generate attribution graphs to reveal internal steps in language models, enabling researchers to trace and visualize circuits.
papers.conclusion: By open-sourcing these tools, the authors aim to advance interpretability research and help the community study model internals, addressing the lag in understanding AI inner workings.
future_direction: Applications of the tools to understand model behaviors
Extensions that improve the tools themselves
papers.abstract: This blog post announces the open-source release of circuit-tracing tools that generate attribution graphs to reveal internal steps in language models, enabling researchers to trace and visualize circuits. By open-sourcing these tools, the authors aim to advance interpretability research and help the community study model internals, addressing the lag in understanding AI inner workings.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
papers.research_question: How can minimal parameter changes, specifically rank-1 LoRAs, be used to understand and interpret the mechanisms behind reasoning capabilities in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Minimal parameter changes via a rank-1 LoRA can recover most reasoning performance and provide interpretable insights, enabling targeted analysis of model behavior.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning capabilities in LLMs can be substantially recovered through minimal parameter modifications, and these changes encode interpretable, reasoning-specific signals, opening new avenues for understanding models via parameter-efficient methods.
papers.key_findings:
A rank-1 LoRA recovers 73-90% of reasoning benchmark performance compared to full finetuning.
LoRA activations are as interpretable as MLP neurons and fire for reasoning-specific behaviors.
Sparse autoencoder on LoRA activations identifies fine-grained, monosemantic features such as Mathematical Operators and Discourse Markers.
MLP adapters contribute more to performance changes than attention adapters, as shown by ablation studies.
The approach demonstrates that parameter-efficient methods can serve as a lens for mechanistic interpretability of reasoning models.
papers.limitation:
Trained on a small dataset (10 million tokens), which may not capture all circuits learned by models trained on larger datasets.
Inconclusive results from steering experiments; large steering magnitudes required, leading to model backtracking.
Heavy reliance on LLM-based autointerpretation methods, which may not uncover the true role of features.
Only one model (Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct) studied, and evaluation focused mostly on math-related reasoning benchmarks.
future_direction: Focused analysis identifying specific circuits that LoRAs interface with to illuminate core computational mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Reasoning models leverage inference-time compute to significantly enhance the performance of language models on difficult logical tasks, and have become a dominating paradigm in frontier LLMs. Despite their wide adoption, the mechanisms underpinning the enhanced performance of these reasoning models are not well understood. In this work, we show that the majority of new capabilities in reasoning models can be elicited by small, single-rank changes to base model parameters, with many of these changes being interpretable. Specifically, we use a rank-1 LoRA to create a minimal parameter adapter for Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct which recovers 73-90% of reasoning-benchmark performance compared to a full parameter finetune. We find that the activations of this LoRA are as interpretable as MLP neurons, and fire for reasoning-specific behaviors. Finally, we train a sparse autoencoder on the entire activation state of this LoRA and identify fine-grained and monosemantic features. Our findings highlight that reasoning performance can arise largely from minimal changes to base model parameters, and explore what these changes affect. More broadly, our work shows that parameter-efficient training methods can be used as a targeted lens for uncovering fundamental insights about language model behavior and dynamics.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Are Your Reasoning Models Reasoning or Guessing? A Mechanistic Analysis of Hierarchical Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) reason? Does it perform gradual reasoning or guessing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic analysis of HRM, revealing that it guesses solutions rather than reasoning incrementally, and proposes data augmentation, input perturbation, and model bootstrapping to improve performance, resulting in Augmented HRM which achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme.
papers.conclusion: HRM guesses rather than reasons, and by understanding this, the authors improve HRM with Augmented HRM, achieving state-of-the-art performance; the analysis provides a qualitative taxonomy for recursive reasoners.
papers.key_findings:
HRM fails on extremely simple puzzles due to violation of the fixed point property, a fundamental assumption of its training.
HRM exhibits 'grokking' dynamics where the answer remains incorrect for many steps then suddenly becomes correct, indicating non-incremental reasoning.
Multiple fixed points (true and false) exist in the latent space, and HRM can get trapped in false fixed points, leading to failure.
HRM appears to be 'guessing' the first fixed point it encounters rather than performing gradual reasoning.
Data augmentation restores the fixed point property, and input perturbation and model bootstrapping improve performance by providing multiple guesses, leading to Augmented HRM with 96.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme.
future_direction: Investigate whether HRM implements an optimization algorithm on a heuristic error metric.
Extend the qualitative taxonomy of reasoning modes to other recursive reasoning models.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical reasoning model (HRM) achieves extraordinary performance on various reasoning tasks, significantly outperforming large language model-based reasoners. To understand the strengths and potential failure modes of HRM, we conduct a mechanistic study on its reasoning patterns and find three surprising facts: (a) Failure of extremely simple puzzles, e.g., HRM can fail on a puzzle with only one unknown cell. We attribute this failure to the violation of the fixed point property, a fundamental assumption of HRM. (b) "Grokking" dynamics in reasoning steps, i.e., the answer is not improved uniformly, but instead there is a critical reasoning step that suddenly makes the answer correct; (c) Existence of multiple fixed points. HRM "guesses" the first fixed point, which could be incorrect, and gets trapped there for a while or forever. All facts imply that HRM appears to be "guessing" instead of "reasoning". Leveraging this "guessing" picture, we propose three strategies to scale HRM's guesses: data augmentation (scaling the quality of guesses), input perturbation (scaling the number of guesses by leveraging inference randomness), and model bootstrapping (scaling the number of guesses by leveraging training randomness). On the practical side, by combining all methods, we develop Augmented HRM, boosting accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme from 54.5% to 96.9%. On the scientific side, our analysis provides new insights into how reasoning models "reason".

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
